intro: Chicago is a young city on old prairie, and its oldest trees are the prairie's survivors: bur oaks that stood here before the city had a name. One shaded the Midway while the 1893 World's Fair rose around it, and a Norwood Park savanna remnant may be older than the United States. Out in the county's forest preserves stand ranked champions, among them a sycamore and a cottonwood both 41.5 metres tall, and oaks of six kinds. The famous zoo oak fell in 2023. Twenty-six of the twenty-eight are free; the two golf-course champions generally need a green fee.
meta_description: Chicago's remarkable trees: prairie bur oaks older than the city, and Cook County's forest preserve champions, from 40-metre cottonwoods to white oaks.
question_meta: Chicago's oldest trees are the bur oaks of Union Ridge Cemetery, estimated at 325 to 375 years. Their story, and 27 more remarkable trees.
question_answer: Chicago's oldest known trees are the bur oaks of the Union Ridge Cemetery savanna in Norwood Park, estimated by one expert survey at 325 to 375 years, older than the United States. The most storied is the bur oak on the Midway Plaisance in Hyde Park, which stood before the 1893 World's Fair was laid out around it.
question_context: Chicago's relationship with old trees is mostly a story of what the prairie kept. The city itself is young, incorporated in 1837, and it burned in 1871, so almost nothing planted stands out for age. What survives is what was already here: bur oaks, the prairie's fire-resistant veterans, in the few corners the city never quite got around to flattening. The best known of them, the bur oak at Lincoln Park Zoo that generations called Chicago's oldest tree, was cut down in May 2023 after it died, which quietly promoted the others. The Midway oak in Hyde Park carries a genuine dispute, one university account says it was planted for the 1893 fair, others say the fair was built around it, and its page gives both versions. The Union Ridge savanna's ages rest on a single expert's estimate and say so. That honesty matters here more than in most cities, because the register Illinois keeps for its champion trees records size, not age, and so does the county's own; a champion is not automatically ancient.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Chicago?
faq.a: The bur oaks of the Union Ridge Cemetery savanna in Norwood Park, estimated at 325 to 375 years by the one expert survey that dated them. The estimate is diameter-based rather than core-based, and the page says so.

faq.q: What happened to the famous oak at Lincoln Park Zoo?
faq.a: The bur oak that was long called Chicago's oldest tree died and was cut down in May 2023. It is not on this list; the trees that are, are the ones you can still stand under.

faq.q: Are Chicago's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Twenty-six of the twenty-eight are free. The Midway oak and the Wooded Island grove stand in public parks, Union Ridge is a cemetery open in daylight hours, and the forest preserve champions stand on public preserve land. The champion boxelder and the champion red pine stand on public golf courses, where a green fee is generally needed to walk the course; ask at the clubhouse.

faq.q: Why are they almost all bur oaks?
faq.a: Because the bur oak is the prairie's survivor: thick corky bark made it the one tree that shrugged off the prairie fires that cleared everything else. What was here before Chicago was mostly bur oak savanna, so what outlived Chicago's building is too.

trees.name: The Bur Oak on the Midway

location.address: Midway Plaisance at Ellis Avenue, Hyde Park, Chicago, IL

trees.story: When the Midway Plaisance was cleared and regraded for the 1893 World's Fair, one tree was left standing, and this is it. By then it was already substantial enough that the ecologist Henry Cowles used it in his 1901 textbook as the example of its kind. Accounts of the fair place it behind the Sitting Bull's Cabin exhibit and the ostrich farm concession, neither of which lasted the year. Sources disagree on how it got here, and it is worth stating both. The University of Chicago Magazine quotes a campus environment official describing it as ostensibly planted as part of a Native American exhibit during the fair itself. The better supported account, from the Hyde Park historian Gary Ossewaarde, from Cowles in 1901 and from a local history record of a 2024 trunk measurement, has it standing long before 1893 and deliberately spared. That measurement reportedly ran past the largest bur oak on the Morton Arboretum's own growth reference chart, which would push it beyond the 250 or so years usually quoted. Bur oak is the tree of the prairie edge in this part of Illinois, corky barked enough to survive the fires that kept the grassland open. This one is the last of that landscape left on the Midway. It stands near Ellis Avenue, in front of the university hospital, on a pin that is close rather than surveyed.
trees.access: Free, public park path along the Midway Plaisance
trees.transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from Millennium Station downtown, then a short walk to Ellis Ave and the Midway

photo.note: Hidde: good photograph of a tree; identity not settled (geotag 86 m from the pin; filename names only the place)

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one big bur oak standing on the open Midway Plaisance at Ellis Avenue, left where it was when everything around it was regraded for the 1893 fair.

trees.name: The Bur Oak Grove of Wooded Island
trees.age_estimate: the grove's oldest survivors are roughly 200 to 300 years

location.address: Wooded Island, Jackson Park, south end near the Clarence Darrow Bridge and Osaka Garden (6200 S. Cornell Ave area), Chicago, IL

trees.story: One of these oaks blew down around 2016, and its rings were counted back to roughly 1730. It had been standing for nearly three centuries when it fell. The ones still up are of the same generation: DNAinfo reported 250 year old bur oaks across the island, with a red oak of about 150 among them. Wooded Island is the part of the 1893 World's Fair that was deliberately left alone. Frederick Law Olmsted kept buildings off it entirely while the Court of Honor went up in white plaster to the south, and fair era painters kept turning their backs on the architecture to paint these oaks instead. The island sits on an undisturbed sand ridge, which is why the soil under the trees was never scraped and rebuilt the way the rest of Jackson Park was. In 2016 the Army Corps of Engineers spent 8.1 million dollars restoring the habitat here and wrote the old bur oaks into the plan, along with roughly 120 bur oak saplings that had seeded themselves around their parents. An oak stand actually reproducing inside a city is a rare thing to stand in. The place to stand is the path just south of the Osaka Garden, looking into the south end of the island, where the grove reads as one thing rather than as scattered trees.

best_time.label: September and October, when the big fringed bur oak acorns come down

trees.access: Free, public park, Chicago Park District (Wooded Island / Osaka Garden)
trees.transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from downtown, then roughly a 15 to 20 minute walk east across Jackson Park to Wooded Island; or CTA bus to the Museum of Science and Industry and cross the Clarence Darrow Bridge
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for a grove rather than one tree: bur oaks of around 250 years with their own saplings seeded around them. Stand on the path just south of the Osaka Garden, at the island's south end.

trees.name: The Bur Oak Savanna of Union Ridge Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: the oldest estimated at 325 to 375 years, based on trunk size

location.address: Union Ridge Cemetery, 6700 W Higgins Ave, Chicago, IL 60656

trees.story: The oldest oak in this grove has been estimated at 325 to 375 years, which would make it roughly two centuries older than the city around it. It was already a mature prairie tree when Chicago was a portage and a fort. The figure comes from Scott Carlini, quoted in a 2016 hunt for the city's oldest tree, and it is based on trunk diameter rather than a ring core, so treat it as directional. We found no second independent estimate, which is why this entry stays flagged. What is solid is the setting. Union Ridge took its first burial in 1841 and is described by the Norwood Park Historical Society as the oldest continuously operating cemetery in Chicago. The ground was open prairie before it was platted, and what stands here is a genuine relict bur oak savanna: widely spaced, heavy limbed trees with daylight between them, which is what oaks look like when they grow up in grassland rather than in forest. Bur oak's thick corky bark let it survive the fires that kept that prairie open, and the graves that arrived in 1841 put an end to both the fires and the plough. It is a working cemetery, so come during posted visiting hours and behave like a guest. The pin is the entrance; the old section and its oaks are inside the grounds.
trees.access: Free, cemetery grounds open to visitors during posted hours
trees.transport: Metra Union Pacific Northwest Line to Norwood Park station, about 22 minutes from Ogilvie Transportation Center downtown, then a short walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for a savanna rather than one tree, widely spaced bur oaks with heavy limbs and daylight between them, which is how oaks grow up in grassland. They stand in Union Ridge Cemetery.

trees.name: The Champion Boxelder of Edgebrook

location.address: Edgebrook Golf Course, 6100 N Central Ave, Chicago, IL 60646 (Forest Preserves of Cook County)

trees.story: Boxelder is the tree nobody wants. It seeds itself into alleys and back lots, drops limbs, hosts the boxelder bugs that get into houses in autumn, and is generally written off as a weed that never lives long enough to get big. This one is the biggest known in Illinois. The state's Big Tree Register, run by University of Illinois Extension, ranks it champion of its species: just over nine feet around the trunk, 55 feet tall, a crown spreading 35 feet, and 172.3 points on the register's scoring formula, ahead of the runner up down in Shawnee National Forest at the far southern end of the state. It was measured and listed in 2026 with a dated photograph, so it is standing now. One honesty note, and it is the reason this entry is flagged: the register is the only source we could find on it. The Sun-Times feature on the state's big trees, the Extension's own announcement and the Forest Preserves champion list all fail to mention it, most likely because the title is very new. No Illinois register carries an age field either, so nobody has dated this tree and we are not going to guess at it. Visiting is a golf question. It stands on Edgebrook Golf Course, a public course run by the Forest Preserves of Cook County, which normally means a green fee to walk the fairways, and whether it can be seen from the perimeter is unconfirmed.
trees.access: Public 18-hole golf course, Forest Preserves of Cook County; a green fee is generally needed to walk the course itself, and whether the tree is visible from a public perimeter trail was not confirmed
trees.transport: Metra Milwaukee District North Line to Edgebrook station, the last stop still inside Chicago city limits, roughly 30 minutes from Chicago Union Station, then about a 15 to 20 minute walk east on Devon/Central Ave to the golf course entrance
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the state-champion box elder, an unusually large specimen of a species normally dismissed as a weed tree, about 2.7m round and 55 feet tall. It stands on Edgebrook Golf Course.

official_register.name: Illinois Big Tree Register (IBTR_masterfile), no. 205

trees.name: The Champion Red Pine of Indian Boundary

location.address: Indian Boundary Golf Course, 8600 W Forest Preserve Ave, Chicago, IL 60634 (Forest Preserves of Cook County)

trees.story: This is the state champion red pine of Illinois, and it holds the title partly for want of competition. The Illinois Big Tree Register lists exactly one red pine anywhere in the state, and this is the one, standing on the Indian Boundary golf course on Chicago's northwest side. Its 153.52 points come from a trunk 6.8 feet around, a height of 64 feet and a crown spreading 31.5 feet, measured and listed in 2026, which doubles as the freshest evidence that it is alive and thriving. Nobody has dated it. Red pine is a northern species, well outside its natural range down here, so this is a planted tree rather than a relic of anything, and the register carries no age field for any entry. Any figure attached to this tree is worked backwards from its trunk rather than measured, and should be read that way. What is documented is the size, and for Pinus resinosa the giveaway is the needles: paired, three to six inches long, snapping cleanly in half when you bend one. Access is the honest problem. Indian Boundary is a public 18 hole course run by the Forest Preserves of Cook County, so walking the fairways generally means paying a green fee, and whether the tree can be seen or reached from outside the course was not established. Ask at the clubhouse before planning the trip.
trees.access: Public 18-hole golf course, Forest Preserves of Cook County; a green fee is generally needed to walk the course itself, and whether the tree is visible from a public perimeter path was not confirmed
trees.transport: Metra Milwaukee District West Line to River Grove or Elmwood Park, roughly 20 minutes from Chicago Union Station; or CTA/Pace bus along Forest Preserve Dr/Cumberland Ave. Exact walk time from the nearest stop to the tree was not verified.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only red pine listed on Illinois' Big Tree Register, paired needles that snap cleanly in half, a trunk about 2m round and 64 feet tall. It stands on Indian Boundary Golf Course.

official_register.name: Illinois Big Tree Register (IBTR_masterfile), no. 207

trees.name: The Kenilworth Witness Oak

location.address: 427 N Kenilworth Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302 (village parkway, Hemingway District)
location.neighbourhood: Oak Park (day trip from Chicago, not within city limits)

trees.story: Local history holds that this bur oak was a witness tree, a landmark the Potawatomi used to find the route back to the Des Plaines River after a hunt. Oak Park's own paper, the Wednesday Journal, reported that reading in 2014 along with the claim that it is the oldest parkway tree in the village. Its age depends on which article you open. The 2014 survey puts it at about 230 years. A 2011 piece in the same paper, written when Openlands and the Morton Arboretum gathered its acorns for a historic oak propagation project, calls it three centuries old. That is a gap of seventy years, nobody has resolved it, and both figures stand here rather than one being quietly chosen. There is a harder caveat. No source has confirmed this tree alive since that 2014 article. In October 2025 another Oak Park heritage bur oak of the same generation, over on Forest Avenue, was removed after disease took it. That was a different tree at a different address, but the cohort is visibly failing, so go expecting an oak and not a guarantee. It stands on the parkway, the village-owned strip between sidewalk and street, in front of a private house on North Kenilworth Avenue in the Hemingway district. Public ground, so stay on the pavement. Oak Park is not Chicago but the suburb immediately west, 20 to 25 minutes from the Loop on the Green Line.
trees.access: Free, public parkway tree (the strip of village-owned land between sidewalk and street), viewable from the public right of way; it fronts a private residence so stay on the parkway/sidewalk
trees.transport: CTA Green Line to Oak Park Ave station, roughly 20 to 25 minutes from the Loop, then about a 10 minute walk north; alternatively Metra Union Pacific West Line to Oak Park station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands, on the village parkway strip between sidewalk and street outside 427 N Kenilworth Avenue. Nobody has confirmed it alive since 2014, so go expecting an oak and not a guarantee.

trees.name: The Sugar Maple of Busse Forest South

location.address: Busse Forest South, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This sugar maple stands 36.6 metres tall, 120 feet, and the Forest Preserves of Cook County rank it second among all the sugar maples on their land. Their champion tree register measured it on 25 August 2023: a trunk 2.47 metres round at chest height, and a crown spreading 22 metres one way and only 12 the other.

That shape is what makes it worth the walk. A trunk under two and a half metres round is slim for a tree of this height, and the narrow crown tells the same story: this maple went up rather than out. Compare the Comfort Maple in Pelham, Ontario, another sugar maple on our map, whose trunk is six metres round. The Busse tree carries well under half that girth, yet the county's champion hackberry at Thatcher Woods, the biggest of its kind on preserve land, is recorded at exactly the same 120 feet.

Busse Forest South holds two more ranked trees: the county's champion basswood, about two and a half kilometres to the west, and its third-ranked basswood a little further north. Three register trees in one preserve make an afternoon of it.

The register records size, rank and place, and nothing about age. Nobody has dated this maple. If you know how old it is, or what stood here before the preserve, tell us. Come in October, when sugar maples colour.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 36.6 metres on a trunk only 2.47 metres round, with a narrow crown. It stands at the register's point in Busse Forest South, about 2.4 km east of the champion basswood.

best_time.label: October, when the sugar maple turns orange and red

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, no. 7

trees.name: The Silver Maple of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Thatcher Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This silver maple's trunk is 4.27 metres round, and in October 2023 the Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it as the second-biggest silver maple on all their land. It stands 26.8 metres tall, with a crown about 18.6 metres across one way and 13 the other.

Four metres of girth is a lot of trunk for a silver maple. On our own map, the Silver Maple of Wołoska in Warsaw measures 3.39 metres round at 20 metres tall, and Bruges' Canada Tree, planted in 1947, measures 2.44. Thicker ones are on our map too, such as one in Warsaw's Park Zaslawa Malickiego at 5.02 metres and Montreal's McKenna Silver Maple at 5.81.

What makes Thatcher Woods unusual is the company. Within 80 metres of this maple the register lists two more ranked trees, both hackberries: the county's champion, and its second-ranked, which at 39 metres is the taller of the two. Three register trees inside one short loop make this the easiest stop of the lot.

The register gives size, rank and place, and nothing more: no planting date, no history, no age. Nobody has dated this maple. If you know how old it is, or have photographs of it from years back, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thick trunk, 4.27 metres round, on a maple about 27 metres tall. It stands in Thatcher Woods roughly 30 metres from the taller second-ranked hackberry.

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, no. 13

trees.name: The Champion Hackberry of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Thatcher Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This is the biggest hackberry the Forest Preserves of Cook County have on their land, ranked first in their champion tree register. Measured in November 2023, it stands 36.6 metres tall on a trunk 3.51 metres round, under a crown about 22 metres wide in both directions.

For scale, the only other hackberry of this species we have measured is the Leaning Hackberry of Parco Treves in Padua: 1.55 metres round and 9 metres tall. The Thatcher Woods champion has more than twice its girth and four times its height.

It is not even the tallest hackberry in these woods. About 66 metres away stands the county's second-ranked hackberry, slimmer at 3.35 metres round but taller at 39 metres. The register still ranks the thicker, wider tree first. A silver maple ranked second in the county stands between the two, so three register trees share one short stretch of woodland.

Another hackberry, at National Grove, matches this trunk exactly at 3.51 metres and ranks third, two and a half metres shorter.

The register says nothing about age, and nobody has dated this tree. If you know how old it is, or have watched it over the years, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad crown, about 22 metres across both ways, over a 3.51 metre trunk. It stands in Thatcher Woods some 66 metres from the taller, slimmer second-ranked hackberry.

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, no. 23

trees.name: The Hackberry of National Grove

location.address: National Grove, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
Of the three hackberries at the top of the Forest Preserves of Cook County's champion register, this one has the widest crown: about 23.5 metres one way and 21.6 the other, measured in December 2023. The register places it third among all the hackberries on preserve land.

Its trunk is 3.51 metres round, exactly the girth of the county champion at Thatcher Woods, about seven kilometres to the north. What separates them is height. The champion stands 36.6 metres, this tree 34.1, and the second-ranked hackberry at Thatcher Woods reaches 39. Three trees of one species, within 16 centimetres of each other in girth and all past 34 metres tall: Cook County grows hackberries big.

The gap with the rest of our map is wider. The only other hackberry of this species we have measured, the Leaning Hackberry of Parco Treves in Padua, is 1.55 metres round and 9 metres tall. National Grove's tree is nearly four times as tall, and its crown spans more than two and a half times the Padua tree's whole height.

Unlike the Thatcher pair, it has no ranked neighbour on our map. It is a stop of its own.

The register records size, rank and site, and no age. Nobody has dated this hackberry. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 23.5 by 21.6 metres, the widest of the county's top three hackberries, over a 3.51 metre trunk. It stands at the register's point in National Grove.

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, no. 26

trees.name: The White Oak of Red Gate Woods

location.address: Red Gate Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
The champion white oak of the Forest Preserves of Cook County is not the thickest white oak they have measured. It wins on everything else. When the register's surveyors measured it in May 2024, they recorded a trunk 4.21 metres round, a height of 29.3 metres and a crown about 23 metres across in both directions, nearly a perfect circle.

The county's second-ranked white oak, at McClaughrey Springs Woods about five kilometres to the southeast, has the fatter trunk at 4.76 metres. It is also eight metres shorter and narrower in the crown, and the register puts Red Gate Woods first.

Our map holds some famous white oaks to measure it against. The Devil's Den Witness Tree at Gettysburg is 4.11 metres round, a whisker thinner than this one. The Ruxton Liberty Tree in Baltimore reaches 5.49 metres and the Travilah Oak outside Washington 5.82. Red Gate Woods' champion does not match those two for girth. What it has is balance: height, trunk and crown together, enough to make it the county's champion.

The register gives size, rank and site, and no age, and girth alone is a poor clock for an oak. Nobody has dated this one. If you know how old it is, or have a core count, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the round, even crown, about 23 metres across both ways, over a 4.21 metre trunk and 29.3 metres of height. It stands at the register's point in Red Gate Woods.

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, no. 111

trees.name: The White Oak of McClaughrey Springs Woods

location.address: McClaughrey Springs Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This white oak is 4.76 metres round at chest height, more than half a metre thicker than the county's champion white oak, and it still ranks second. The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it in June 2024.

What it lacks is height. The champion at Red Gate Woods, about five kilometres to the northwest, is thinner at 4.21 metres but stands 29.3 metres tall. This one stops at 21, with a crown about 21 metres one way and 17 the other. Short and heavy against tall and even: the register prefers the second, a visitor may well prefer the first.

For comparison, the Devil's Den Witness Tree at Gettysburg, another white oak on our map, is 4.11 metres round. The Ruxton Liberty Tree in Baltimore, at 5.49, and the Travilah Oak near Washington, at 5.82, are bigger still, but McClaughrey Springs' oak is in that company.

The surveyors left two notes. It stands at the edge of a trail, which makes it easy to reach. And it shows some branch dieback, which is worth knowing before you go and worth telling us about if you see it worsen.

The register gives no age, and nobody has dated this oak. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.76 metres round, on a short oak of 21 metres with some dead branches. It stands at the edge of a trail in McClaughrey Springs Woods.

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, no. 169

trees.name: The Sassafras of Thorn Creek Division

location.address: Thorn Creek Division, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This sassafras is only 12.2 metres tall, and its trunk is 3.26 metres round. That makes it the biggest sassafras the Forest Preserves of Cook County have on their land, ranked first in their champion register when it was measured in July 2024.

Those two numbers sit oddly together, which is the reason to go. Set it beside another tree on our Chicago page, the county's second-ranked sugar maple at Busse Forest South: the maple is three times as tall, at 36.6 metres, and its trunk is thinner, at 2.47. The sassafras put its growth into girth. The crown follows suit, about 13 metres one way and 9 the other, low and compact over a trunk that would look at home on a tree twice its height.

It stands far from the other champions on this page, at Thorn Creek Division in southern Cook County, so it is a trip of its own rather than a stop on a walk.

The only other sassafras on our map stands in Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn, and we hold no measurement for it, so for now this is the one with numbers.

The register gives no age, and nobody has dated this tree. If you know how old it is, tell us. Come in October, when sassafras turns orange and red.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thick trunk, 3.26 metres round, on a low tree only about 12 metres tall with a compact crown. It stands at the register's point in Thorn Creek Division.

best_time.label: October, when the mitten-shaped leaves turn orange and red

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, no. 200

trees.name: The Champion Basswood of Busse Forest South

location.address: Busse Forest South, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This is the biggest basswood on all the land of the Forest Preserves of Cook County, first in their champion tree register. Its trunk is 3.91 metres round, and it stands 24.4 metres tall under a crown about 16 metres one way and 17 the other.

The same preserve holds the county's third-ranked basswood, about 730 metres to the north, and the two are an instructive pair. They are exactly the same height, 24.4 metres each. The difference is all in the trunk: this one is 80 centimetres thicker round, and the register ranks it first and the other third. Stand at one and then the other, and you are looking at the same species, the same height and the same woods, with the champion simply carrying more wood.

Busse Forest South holds a third ranked tree as well, the county's second-ranked sugar maple, about two and a half kilometres to the east and twelve metres taller than either basswood. Together they make a long walk past three trees the county has measured and ranked.

The register records the size and place but no measurement date, and nothing about age. Nobody has dated this basswood. If you know how old it is, or when it was last measured, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 3.91 metres round, the thicker of the two ranked basswoods in Busse Forest South. It stands about 730 metres south of the third-ranked one, at the register's point.

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, no. 263

trees.name: The Third-Ranked Basswood of Busse Forest South

location.address: Busse Forest South, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This basswood is the third biggest the Forest Preserves of Cook County have measured on their land, and it stands just 730 metres from the champion. The two are exactly the same height, 24.4 metres each.

Where they part is the trunk. This one is 3.11 metres round against the champion's 3.91. Its crown, though, is the wider of the two, about 19 metres one way and 16 the other, so from a distance it may look the larger tree. Up close, the trunk tells them apart, and the register ranks this one third.

That makes Busse Forest South a good place to train your eye. Walk between the two basswoods and you see how much a species can vary in one woodland: same height, same ground, eighty centimetres of trunk between them. The preserve's other ranked tree, the county's second-ranked sugar maple, stands about two and a half kilometres to the southeast and rises to 36.6 metres, half as tall again as either basswood.

The register records size and place but no date of measurement and no age. Nobody has dated this tree. If you know how old it is, or have measured it yourself, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wide crown, about 19 by 16 metres, over a trunk 3.11 metres round, slimmer than the champion's. It stands about 730 metres north of the champion basswood.

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, no. 264

trees.name: The Pin Oak of Rolling Knolls

location.address: Rolling Knolls, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This pin oak's crown spreads about 26 metres one way and 22 the other, on a tree only 29 metres tall. It is the champion pin oak of the Forest Preserves of Cook County, first among all those on preserve land, and it is nearly as wide as it is high.

The trunk is 3.59 metres round. Put the tree beside the county's champion white oak at Red Gate Woods, itself notable for a broad, even crown: that oak is 29.3 metres tall, almost the same, yet its crown is about three metres narrower across its widest line. Only three Cook County trees on our Chicago page spread further: the champion sycamore at Riverside Lawn, and the bur oak and silver maple of Harms Woods and Harms Flatwoods, each about 27 metres across.

Pin oaks are familiar on our map from the other side of the Atlantic. We list them in Dutch parks in Haarlem, Apeldoorn, Eindhoven and Sittard, where the registers record planting dates between the 1860s and about 1910. None of those carries a measured trunk or crown on our pages, so this champion is the first pin oak we can describe in numbers.

Rolling Knolls lies at the far western edge of the trees on this page, a trip of its own rather than part of a walk.

The register records no measurement date and no age. Nobody has dated this oak. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 26 by 22 metres, nearly as wide as the 29-metre tree is tall, over a trunk 3.59 metres round. It stands at the register's point in Rolling Knolls.

trees.name: The Cottonwood of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Entrance on Chicago Ave, west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest, IL 60305, Forest Preserves of Cook County

trees.access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/thatcher-woods/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
trees.transport: Entrance Chicago Ave west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest; public transport not verified.
trees.story:
At 41.5 metres, this cottonwood shares the title of tallest tree anyone has measured on our Chicago map with the sycamore at Riverside Lawn, and the Forest Preserves of Cook County still rank it only second among their cottonwoods.

The trunk is just as far out of scale. Measured in July 2023, it is 5.94 metres round, the thickest recorded girth on this page. The crown is far from round: about 28 metres one way and only 17 the other. Somewhere else on preserve land stands a cottonwood the register puts ahead of it.

It also anchors the best short walk on the page. About 130 metres to the north stands the county's second-ranked silver maple, and just beyond it the two ranked hackberries, the champion and its taller runner-up. A third-ranked bitternut hickory stands about 400 metres to the south-east. That is five register trees inside roughly 600 metres of the same woods.

The nearest rival in size is another cottonwood, at National Grove about seven kilometres south: 5.82 metres round, 39 metres tall, and ranked third.

Everything here comes from one source, the county's champion tree register, which records size, rank and place. It says nothing about age. Nobody has dated this cottonwood. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 41.5 metres tall on a trunk 5.94 metres round, the biggest of the ranked trees in Thatcher Woods. It stands about 130 metres south of the second-ranked silver maple.

trees.name: The Second-Ranked Hackberry of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Entrance on Chicago Ave, west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest, IL 60305, Forest Preserves of Cook County

trees.access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/thatcher-woods/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
trees.transport: Entrance Chicago Ave west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest; public transport not verified.
trees.story:
This hackberry stands 2.4 metres taller than the county's champion hackberry, 66 metres away, and the register still ranks it second.

At 39 metres, 128 feet, it is the tallest of the three hackberries at the top of the Forest Preserves of Cook County's champion register. The champion beats it everywhere else: 3.51 metres round against this tree's 3.35, and a crown about 22 metres across both ways against this one's 19.5 by 15.5. The register crowns the stout tree, not the tall one.

For a sense of what 39 metres means for the species, the only other common hackberry we have measured, the Leaning Hackberry of Parco Treves in Padua, is 9 metres tall. This one is more than four times that.

The pair is the reason to come. Stand between them and you see one species on one patch of ground grown two ways, one taller and one stouter. The county's second-ranked silver maple stands about 30 metres to the south, and the second-ranked cottonwood, at 41.5 metres the one ranked tree here taller still, about 160 metres south.

The register gives no date for this measurement and no age. It is the only source for the tree. Nobody has dated this hackberry. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 39 metres, taller and slimmer than the champion hackberry 66 metres away. It stands about 30 metres north of the second-ranked silver maple.

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, record 307

trees.name: The Bitternut Hickory of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Entrance on Chicago Ave, west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest, IL 60305, Forest Preserves of Cook County

trees.access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/thatcher-woods/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
trees.transport: Entrance Chicago Ave west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest; public transport not verified.
trees.story:
This bitternut hickory stands 34 metres tall on a trunk only 1.92 metres round, about 61 centimetres across.

That is a lot of tree on a slim stem. The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it in November 2023 and ranked it third among the bitternut hickories on their land. Its height, 34.1 metres, matches the third-ranked hackberry at National Grove to the decimetre, on a trunk little more than half that tree's girth.

Bitternut is a tree we rarely get to show. The only other one on our map grows in Ottawa's Dominion Arboretum, where it was planted between 1886 and 1890 and no girth is recorded. This one has measurements and no history; that one has history and no measurements.

In Thatcher Woods it sits at the south-east end of the preserve's ranked trees: about 400 metres from the second-ranked cottonwood and about 580 metres from the champion hackberry. Walk the group from north to south and the hickory is where you finish.

The county's champion register is the only source for it. It records size, rank and the measurement date, and nothing on age. Nobody has dated this hickory. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the slender trunk, 1.92 metres round, on a tree 34 metres tall. It stands about 400 metres south-east of the second-ranked cottonwood, the southernmost of the ranked trees in Thatcher Woods.

trees.name: The Chinkapin Oak of National Grove

location.address: National Grove North entrance W 26th St east of 1st Ave, North Riverside, IL 60546, Forest Preserves of Cook County

trees.access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/national-grove/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
trees.transport: North entrance W 26th St east of 1st Ave, North Riverside; public transport not verified.
trees.story:
This is the only chinkapin oak on our map, and it happens to be the biggest one the Forest Preserves of Cook County have found on all their land.

The county measured it in July 2024 and ranked it first of its species in their champion tree register. Its trunk is 3.72 metres round, and it stands 29.3 metres tall, exactly the height of the county's champion white oak at Red Gate Woods. Its crown spreads about 25 metres one way and 23 the other, close to round, a fraction narrower than the champion pin oak's at Rolling Knolls.

The point of coming to National Grove is that it does not stand alone. About 240 metres to the south is the county's third-ranked hackberry, and about 125 metres beyond that the third-ranked cottonwood, 5.82 metres round and 39 metres tall. Three ranked trees of three different species in under 400 metres make this the second walk on the page, after Thatcher Woods to the north.

Of those three, the oak is the only champion. That title is about size on preserve land, not age, and the register keeps no age for any of its trees. It is also the only source for this one. Nobody has dated this oak. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only oak among National Grove's ranked trees, a trunk 3.72 metres round under a crown about 25 by 23 metres. It stands about 240 metres north of the third-ranked hackberry.

trees.name: The Cottonwood of National Grove

location.address: National Grove North entrance W 26th St east of 1st Ave, North Riverside, IL 60546, Forest Preserves of Cook County

trees.access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/national-grove/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
trees.transport: North entrance W 26th St east of 1st Ave, North Riverside; public transport not verified.
trees.story:
Ranked only third among Cook County's forest preserve cottonwoods, this tree has a trunk 5.82 metres round, the thickest recorded on our Chicago map bar one.

The exception is its rival at Thatcher Woods, about seven kilometres north. The two are close enough to be twins on paper: 12 centimetres of girth and 2.5 metres of height between them, this one at 39 metres, 128 feet, and the Thatcher tree at 41.5. The register still sets a full ranked place between them.

To see how far out of line these cottonwoods are, set this one beside the oaks. The thickest white oak on this page, the county's second-ranked tree at McClaughrey Springs Woods, is 4.76 metres round, more than a metre thinner. The champion chinkapin oak a few hundred metres north of here manages 3.72.

The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it on 21 December 2023, the same day as the third-ranked hackberry, which stands about 125 metres to the north-north-east. With the chinkapin oak beyond that, it makes the southern end of a short line of three ranked trees in National Grove.

The register is the only source for this tree, and it records size and rank but not age. Nobody has dated this cottonwood. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.82 metres round, far thicker than the hackberry nearby, on a tree 39 metres tall. It stands about 125 metres south-south-west of the third-ranked hackberry.

trees.name: The Bur Oak of Harms Woods

location.address: Harms Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.story:
Cook County's third-ranked bur oak has a trunk 4.83 metres round, to the centimetre the girth we list for the Kile Oak, Indianapolis's best-known tree.

The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it on 1 August 2023: 24.4 metres tall, 80 feet, under a crown about 27 metres one way and 22 the other, so the tree is wider than it is high. Two bur oaks on preserve land rank above it.

Bur oak is the tree Chicago's oldest stories hang on. The Midway oak, the Wooded Island grove and the Union Ridge savanna on this page are all bur oaks, and none of them carries a measured trunk. This one is the reverse: numbers, and no history. Harms Woods is an oak woodland and an Illinois Nature Preserve, so this oak stands among others of its kind rather than alone on a lawn.

It also makes a pair. About 820 metres to the north-east, in Harms Flatwoods, stands the county's champion silver maple, the thickest silver maple in the register. One walk takes in both.

The register is the only source for this oak. It records size, rank and the day of measurement, and says nothing about age, and girth alone is a poor clock for an oak. Nobody has dated it. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.83 metres round, under a crown about 27 by 22 metres, wider than the tree is tall. It stands in Harms Woods, about 820 metres south-west of the champion silver maple.

trees.name: The Sycamore of Riverside Lawn

location.address: Riverside Lawn, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.story:
Score Cook County's forest preserve champions the way the county does, and this sycamore beats every other tree in the register.

The Forest Preserves of Cook County add a tree's trunk in inches, its height in feet and a quarter of its average crown width. This one comes to 313.86 points, the highest total they record. In metres: a trunk 3.91 round, a height of 41.5, and a crown about 30 metres one way and 28 the other. It shares the title of tallest tree on our Chicago map with the Thatcher Woods cottonwood, and no crown on this page spreads wider.

No sycamore we list anywhere is taller. The Brandywine Sycamore in Pennsylvania and the Sunderland Buttonball Tree in Massachusetts are far thicker, but neither reaches 35 metres. The nearest in height, at Valley Garden Park in Wilmington, stops at 39.6.

The county measured it on 9 February 2024, in midwinter. Riverside Lawn is a Forest Preserves site beside the Des Plaines River, in the village of Riverside; Metra's Riverside station on the BNSF line lies about 1.1 kilometres away in a straight line. National Grove's three ranked trees stand about two kilometres to the north-west, close enough to make one outing of it.

The register is the only source for this tree. It ranks and measures, and records no age. Nobody has dated this sycamore. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 41.5 metres tall under a crown about 30 metres across, on a trunk 3.91 metres round. It stands at the register's point in Riverside Lawn, the preserve beside the Des Plaines River.

trees.name: The Black Oak of Willow Springs Woods

location.address: Willow Springs Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.story:
The champion black oak of the Forest Preserves of Cook County stands 36.6 metres tall, the tallest oak on our Chicago map, on a crown barely 14 metres across.

That is the shape to come for. The county measured it on 24 July 2023: a trunk 3.63 metres round, 120 feet of height, and a crown about 14 metres one way and 12.5 the other. Every other measured oak on this page is shorter and spreads wider. The champion pin oak at Rolling Knolls is more than seven metres lower with a crown nearly twice as broad, and the champion white oak at Red Gate Woods, about 3.7 kilometres to the south-west, tops out at 29.3.

It is also the first black oak on our map anywhere, and it arrives as the biggest one the county has found on its land, ranked first of its species.

Willow Springs Woods pairs it with a neighbour. About 1.8 kilometres to the east-south-east, in Spears Woods, stands the county's second-ranked swamp white oak, measured on the same July day. The two oaks could hardly be built more differently: this one tall and narrow, that one about as wide as it is high.

The register is the only source for this tree. It gives size, rank and the date, and no age. Nobody has dated this oak. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 36.6 metres, over a narrow crown only about 14 by 12.5 metres, on a trunk 3.63 metres round. It stands at the register's point in Willow Springs Woods.

trees.name: The American Elm of Schiller Woods

location.address: Schiller Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.story:
Dutch elm disease has made an American elm with a trunk four metres round an uncommon thing, and the county's register puts one in Schiller Woods, 4.07 metres round, ranked only third of its kind.

The Forest Preserves of Cook County list it at 25.6 metres tall, 84 feet, in their champion tree register. Two American elms on preserve land rank above it, and neither is on our map. Elsewhere we list bigger ones still: the elm at the East 97th Street entrance to Central Park and the Smithsonian's Witness Elm in Washington are both over 5.4 metres round. Against Montreal's Last Elm of Mont-Royal, at 3.46, this one is the heavier tree.

This entry comes with more caveats than most on the page, and they are worth knowing before you set out. The register row carries no measurement date, so we cannot say when the tape went round it, and no second source confirms the size. The record was last edited in February 2025, which is the latest sign we have that the tree stands. And the pin is the register's point, close but not checked against the crown, so look for the trunk rather than the dot.

Schiller Woods lies about 1.5 kilometres north of the champion red pine at Indian Boundary.

Nobody has dated this elm. If you have seen it, measured it or know its age, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 4.07 metres round, large for an American elm, on a tree about 25.6 metres tall. It stands in Schiller Woods near the register's point, which is approximate.

trees.name: The Bald Cypress of McGinnis Slough

location.address: McGinnis Slough, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.story:
Two of the three biggest bald cypresses on Cook County's forest preserve land stand about 50 metres apart, in the same slough.

This is the stouter of them, and the register ranks it second of its species: a trunk 3.78 metres round on a tree 20 metres tall, 65.6 feet, measured on 24 July 2023. Its neighbour, ranked third, grows the other way, with a trunk about 3.2 metres round and a height of about 25.6. Stand between them and you see one species on one patch of wet ground making two different trees.

The numbers have a near twin across the Atlantic. The bald cypress at the Monnikendam in Amersfoort, on our Dutch pages, is 3.81 metres round and 20 metres tall, within three centimetres of this one.

Whether these cypresses were planted or came up on their own, the register does not say, and neither do we. What it does record is size, rank and the day of measurement, the same July day the county measured the champion black oak at Willow Springs Woods and the swamp white oak at Spears Woods, both nine to ten kilometres to the north.

Come in autumn. Bald cypress is a conifer that drops its needles, and before they fall they turn copper red.

The register is the only source and gives no age. Nobody has dated this tree. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the thicker of the two ranked bald cypresses in McGinnis Slough, 3.78 metres round and 20 metres tall. The other, about 50 metres away, is taller and slimmer.

best_time.label: October and November, when the soft needles turn copper red and then fall

trees.name: The Swamp White Oak of Spears Woods

location.address: Spears Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.story:
This swamp white oak is very nearly as wide as it is tall: a crown about 21 metres across in both directions, on a tree 21.9 metres high.

The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it on 24 July 2023 and ranked it second among the swamp white oaks on their land. The trunk is 3.38 metres round, 133 inches. The crown is about 21.3 metres one way and 20.4 the other, close to a circle.

Our map holds two other swamp white oaks, the Sickles Witness Tree on the Gettysburg battlefield and one at the North Lookout in Ottawa, and neither carries a measured trunk on our pages. This one is the opposite case: a tree with a tape measure on it and no story behind it yet.

Spears Woods makes a pair with Willow Springs Woods, about 1.8 kilometres to the west-north-west, where the county's champion black oak stands. The county measured both on the same day, and they could hardly look less alike: this oak low and round, that one 36.6 metres tall on a crown only about 14 metres across. A third tree measured that day, the second-ranked bald cypress at McGinnis Slough, stands about nine kilometres south.

The register is the only source for this oak, and it records no age. Nobody has dated it. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the round crown, about 21 metres across both ways, as wide as the 21.9-metre tree is tall, over a trunk 3.38 metres round. It stands at the register's point in Spears Woods.

trees.name: The Silver Maple of Harms Flatwoods

location.address: Harms Flatwoods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.story:
Cook County's champion silver maple beats the runner-up in Thatcher Woods by five centimetres of trunk.

The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it on 1 August 2023: 4.32 metres round, 170 inches, the thickest silver maple in their champion register, and 24.9 metres tall. The Thatcher Woods maple, ranked second, has 4.27 metres of trunk and is about two metres taller. This one makes up for it in the crown, about 27 metres one way and 22 the other, against the Thatcher tree's 18.6 by 13.

Two Dutch silver maples on our map come within a hair of it: the one in Tilburg's Leijpark is 4.30 metres round and the one at Gripper in Oss 4.31.

Harms Flatwoods is an Illinois Nature Preserve. Visitors keep to the trails, and we cannot yet tell you whether this tree can be seen from one. If you find it from a trail, tell us where you stood; that is the most useful thing anyone could add to this page.

About 820 metres to the south-west, in Harms Woods, stands the county's third-ranked bur oak, close enough to make the two one walk.

The register is the only source and gives no age. Nobody has dated this maple. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.32 metres round, under a crown about 27 by 22 metres. It stands in Harms Flatwoods, about 820 metres north-east of the third-ranked bur oak in Harms Woods.
